instruction: Tell me a myth about "Aengus".
output: Aengus's mythology is a study in winning without fighting. The three great set-pieces — his birth inside a stopped day, his taking of the Brug, and the dream-quest for Caer Ibormeith — are all victories of time: time held still, time parsed, time waited out. Cath Maige Tuired and Tochmarc Étaíne add the counselor and the host: the son whose wit saves his father, and the keeper of the Brug who shelters Étaín when the whole of Ireland has no safer room. [Tochmarc Étaíne] The Day the Sun Stood Still: The Dagda desired Bóand, the wife of Elcmar of the Brug, and sent Elcmar away on a day's errand to Bres. To hide what followed, the tale says, the Dagda made the sun stand still: nine months passed, and the world reckoned it a single day — so the child was conceived and born within one day, and Elcmar came home none the wiser. They named the boy Óengus, but the story gave him the name that stuck: mac ind Óc, 'the son of the young', because young was the day that bore him. The episode fixes the god's signature before he can speak: he is a child of bent time. Bóand, the Boyne itself made goddess, is his mother; the Dagda, the All-Father, his sire; and his first house is the river-bend his father stole a day to give him. The fosterage that followed — with Midir of Brí Léith — placed him among the proudest of the Túatha Dé Danann and set up every tale that came after. [De Gabáil in t-Sída] A Day and a Night: When the Dagda divided the síd-mounds of Ireland among the Túatha Dé Danann, Óengus was away fostered with Midir and received nothing. He came home to claim his share, and the Dagda, having no mound left to give, granted him Brú na Bóinne — the Dagda's own house — for a day and a night. When the term was spent and the Dagda asked for his Brug back, Óengus answered that it is in days and nights that the whole world is spent, and so the grant had no end. The All-Father lost the argument, and the greatest mound in Ireland passed to the son who had read the fine print. The tale is told with a straight face, but its logic is the logic of the síd itself: the Otherworld does not run on mortal clocks. A god born inside a single stretched day is the natural owner of a house held on a day without a term. Irish law prized the exact word; Óengus's first deed makes etymology into real estate. [Aislinge Óenguso] The Dream of Óengus: A maiden came to Óengus in sleep, playing a timpán, the sweetest music he had heard; for a year she came, and for a year he could not touch her, and when she ceased to come he wasted with love-sickness. The physicians of the Túatha Dé Danann could not cure him, for his sickness was a woman who existed somewhere in the world. Bóand his mother searched Ireland for a year and found nothing; the Dagda searched a year and found nothing; then Bodb Derg, king of the síd of Munster, searched, and at the year's end found her: Caer Ibormeith, daughter of Ethal Anbuail of síd Uaman in Connacht. But Caer lived under a rhythm no bargain could break: she spent one year in girl's shape and one as a swan, among nine score swans on Loch Bél Dracon, and the change came at Samain. Óengus went to the lake at Samain and saw them, each pair of swans linked by a silver chain, Caer's own chain of gold about her neck. He called to her, and she answered that she would go with him only if he took the swan-shape beside her. He entered the water, became a swan, and they flew three times around the lake — and their music put every listener to sleep for three days and three nights — then away to Brú na Bóinne, where the singing of the two swans became part of the mound's music ever after. [Tochmarc Étaíne] The Bower of the Purple Fly: When the jealous Fuamnach struck Étaín with a rod of scarlet quicken-tree and made her a pool of water, then a worm, then a purple fly, the fly that was Étaín came at last to Brú na Bóinne, to the hall of Óengus. He knew her — the fly's music and its radiance were hers — and he built her a grianán, a sun-bower of crystal filled with healing herbs and the bloom of every field, and she stayed with him there, and the window of the bower let her pass in and out as she pleased. It could not last. Fuamnach followed the rumor of the fly's good fortune and raised a magic wind that swept Étaín out of the bower and across Ireland for seven years, until she fell into the cup of Étar's wife at the Bay of Cíú and was drunk, conceived, and born again a thousand and twelve years after her first birth. Óengus's shelter is one of the gentlest episodes in the cycle: the young god keeping one hunted woman safe in the safest house in Ireland, against a malice even his Brug could not finally exclude. [Cath Maige Tuired] The Satirist's Three Gold Coins: Under the tyranny of Bres the Dagda was set to building the usurper's forts, and the satirist Cridenbél taxed him the three best bits of every ration, until the greatest of the gods was failing from hunger — for no one dared refuse a satirist whose curse raised blisters on the face. Óengus came to his father and gave him the counsel that turned the trap: demand of Bres the pick of the cattle of Ireland as wages, and hide three gold coins in the porridge portion meant for the satirist. Cridenbél swallowed greed and gold together and died of it; and when Bres demanded the Dagda's death for the killing, the dead man's own belly gave the verdict — cut open, it held the gold, proof that greed and not the Dagda had killed him. The episode is the tradition's clearest pairing of father and son: the Dagda's patience carrying the labor, Óengus's wit carrying the case. The young god does not raise a weapon in the whole of Cath Maige Tuired, and does not need to — his contribution to the war that freed the Túatha Dé Danann was a sentence spoken at the right fireside.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Rhiannon".
output: Rhiannon is the strongest female figure in the Four Branches of the Mabinogi, and the tales give her a complete arc: the uncatchable rider who chooses her husband, the accused mother who bears her penance, the captive of the enchantment who comes home still a queen. Every word of her story is medieval Welsh prose, preserved in two great manuscripts. [First Branch · Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed] The Rider on the Pale Horse: Pwyll, prince of Dyfed, goes up to Gorsedd Arberth, the mound where a man either suffers blows or sees a wonder, and there he sees a lady in shining gold brocade riding past on a great pale horse — at a slow, even pace. He sends his swiftest rider after her; the faster the pursuit, the farther she draws ahead. Day after day it happens, with Pwyll's own horse and Pwyll himself, until at last he calls out: 'Maiden, for the sake of the man you love best, wait for me.' She stops at once: 'I will wait gladly — and it would have been better for the horse had you asked me that long ago.' She is Rhiannon, daughter of Hefaidd Hên, and she has come of her own will: she is being given to a man she does not want, and she has chosen Pwyll instead. [First Branch · Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed] The Bag That Would Not Fill: At the wedding feast, Pwyll grants a request before he hears it — and the petitioner is Gwawl fab Clud, the suitor Rhiannon refused, who claims her by the promise. Rhiannon is not dismayed; she devises the counter-plot. A year later Pwyll comes to Gwawl's feast disguised as a beggar, asking only that a certain small bag she has given him be filled with food. The bag cannot be filled: it will never be full, she has told him, unless a true lord treads the food down with his feet and declares that enough has been put in. Gwawl rises and treads it down — and Pwyll draws the bag shut over him, blows his horn, and his war-band falls on the hall. Each man strikes the bag and asks what is in it; 'a badger,' comes the answer, and from that night the Welsh played the game called Badger in the Bag. Gwawl buys his release with sureties and a renounced claim, and Rhiannon marries the man she chose. [First Branch · Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed] The May-Eve Vanishing and the Penance: After three childless years the nobles of Dyfed press Pwyll to take another wife; he begs one year more, and Rhiannon bears a son. On the night of the birth the six women set to watch all fall asleep, and the child is gone. Terrified of the blame, the women kill the pups of a hound, smear the blood on Rhiannon's face, lay the bones beside her, and swear she has destroyed her own child. Pwyll will not put her away, but a penance is imposed: she is to sit beside the horse-block at the gate of Arberth, tell her story to every traveller who comes, and offer to carry guests and strangers to the court on her back. She accepts the sentence she did not earn, and she bears it without breaking. The child, meanwhile, has fallen into the strangest rescue in Welsh prose. Teyrnon Twrf Liant, a lord by the sea, loses a foal every May-eve; keeping watch over his mare, he sees a great clawed hand reach through the window to seize the newborn foal, and strikes it off with his sword. Outside the door he finds a baby wrapped in silk brocade. He and his wife rear the boy as Gwri Wallt Euryn, Gwri of the Golden Hair — who grows with uncanny speed and bears, year by year, the very likeness of Pwyll. When Teyrnon hears of Rhiannon's penance, he knows what he must do, and he and his wife bring the boy to Arberth. Rhiannon looks at him and says that if this is true, her pryder — her care, her anxiety — is lifted from her. From that word the boy is named Pryderi, and the penance ends. [Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr] The Enchantment of Dyfed and the Collars of Asses: After Pwyll's death, Rhiannon is given in marriage to Manawydan fab Llŷr, and the four of them — Rhiannon and Manawydan, Pryderi and his wife Cigfa — return to Dyfed. There comes a peal of thunder and a fall of mist, and when it lifts, the land is emptied: not a person, not a dwelling, not a beast remains. For two years the four live by hunting; then they try their hand at saddlery, shield-making, and shoemaking in the towns of England, and each time the local craftsmen drive them out for making work too good to allow. Back in empty Dyfed, a shining white boar leads Pryderi and Manawydan to a fortress that was never there before; Pryderi goes in, lays hold of a golden bowl hanging by chains above a marble fountain, and is rooted to the spot, struck dumb. Rhiannon goes in after him, takes hold of the same bowl, and is trapped beside him — and fort, bowl, and both prisoners vanish. Manawydan undoes the spell by patience. Sowing wheat, he watches three ripe fields stripped bare by mice on successive nights, and on the third he catches one slow, heavy mouse and condemns it to hang as a thief. A clerk, a priest, and a bishop come one after another to beg it off, each offering more than the last, and Manawydan names his price: Pryderi and Rhiannon released, the enchantment lifted from Dyfed, and no vengeance taken. The mouse is the wife of Llwyd fab Cilcoed, transformed with all his household; Llwyd had laid the spell to avenge his friend Gwawl fab Clud. Pryderi comes home with the gate-hammer about his neck, and Rhiannon with the collars of asses about hers — the second humiliation she has worn like a queen, and the second she survives. [Second Branch · Branwen ferch Llŷr] The Birds of Rhiannon: Rhiannon never steps on stage in the Second Branch, but her birds do. When the seven survivors of the Irish war come back over the sea bearing the wounded head of Brân the Blessed, they feast at Harlech for seven years, and there come three birds — the Birds of Rhiannon, Adar Rhiannon — that begin to sing to them. Every other song seems unlovely beside it; and though the birds must be gazed at far out over the sea, their singing is as clear as if they sang in the hall. At Gwales in Penfro the company feasts on for eighty years with the uncorrupted head, in the presence of the birds' song, until the door toward Cornwall is opened and memory and sorrow return. Later Welsh tradition says of the Adar Rhiannon that their song wakes the dead and lulls the living to sleep — the music of a world that does not end.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Pryderi".
output: Pryderi's mythology is unique in Welsh prose: he is the only character who appears in all Four Branches of the Mabinogi, and his life is the thread the whole cycle is strung on. The First Branch gives his birth, theft, and naming; the Second carries him through the Irish war as one of the seven survivors; the Third empties his kingdom and takes him captive; the Fourth kills him. Every word of it is medieval Welsh prose, preserved in two great manuscripts. [First Branch · Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed] The May-Eve Vanishing: Pryderi is born to Pwyll and Rhiannon after the nobles of Dyfed have pressed for an heir, and on the night of his birth the six women set to watch all fall asleep — and the child is gone. Terrified of the blame, the women kill the pups of a hound, smear the blood on Rhiannon's face, lay the bones beside her, and swear she has destroyed her own son; her penance at the horse-block begins, and it will last until the boy comes home. The child, meanwhile, has fallen into the strangest rescue in Welsh prose. Teyrnon Twrf Liant, a lord of Gwent Is Coed by the sea, loses a foal every May-eve; keeping watch over his mare, he sees a great clawed hand reach through the window to seize the newborn foal, and strikes it off with his sword. Outside the door he finds a baby boy wrapped in silk brocade. He and his wife rear the child as their own and call him Gwri Wallt Euryn — Gwri of the Golden Hair. [First Branch · Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed] The Naming at Arberth: Gwri grows with uncanny speed — at the end of his first year sturdier than a child of three, at two like a boy of six — and year by year he bears the very likeness of Pwyll. When Teyrnon hears of Rhiannon's penance, he knows what he must do, and he and his wife bring the boy to Arberth. The court sees the likeness at once, and Rhiannon says that if this is true, her pryder — her care, her anxiety — is lifted from her. Pwyll declares that the boy should take his name from the word his mother spoke when the news was brought to her, and so the child is named Pryderi. The penance ends; Teyrnon will take no reward beyond the boy's friendship; and Pryderi is fostered with Pendaran Dyfed until he is of age, when Pwyll gives him the realm. [Second Branch · Branwen ferch Llŷr] One of the Seven: When Bendigeidfran — Brân the Blessed — leads the host of Britain into Ireland to answer the wrong done to Branwen, the war ends in near-total ruin: the Irish are destroyed, and of the host of the Island of the Mighty only seven men come back alive, bearing Brân's wounded head. The tale names them, and the first two it names are Pryderi and Manawydan, with Glifieu, Taliesin, Ynawg, Gruddieu, and Heilyn. With the others Pryderi feasts seven years at Harlech, where the Birds of Rhiannon sing, and eighty years at Gwales in Penfro in the Assembly of the Wondrous Head — a man who has sailed out of his own branch into the middle of someone else's tragedy, and who carries its grief home into the Third. [Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr] The Enchantment of Dyfed: After Pwyll's death, Pryderi rules Dyfed and gives his mother Rhiannon in marriage to Manawydan fab Llŷr; with his wife Cigfa, the four come home to Arberth. There comes a peal of thunder and a fall of mist, and when it lifts, Dyfed is emptied — not a person, not a dwelling, not a beast remains. For two years the four live by hunting; then they try saddlery, shield-making, and shoemaking in the towns of England, and each time the local craftsmen drive them out for making work too good to allow. Back in empty Dyfed, a shining white boar leads Pryderi and Manawydan to a fortress that was never there before. Against Manawydan's counsel Pryderi goes in, lays hold of a golden bowl hanging by chains above a marble fountain — and his hands stick to the bowl, his feet to the slab, and speech leaves him. Rhiannon goes in after him, takes hold of the same bowl, and is caught beside him; fort, bowl, and both prisoners vanish. Manawydan undoes the spell by patience: sowing wheat, he catches the one slow mouse stripping his third ripe field, condemns it to hang as a thief, and names his price to the bishop who comes to beg it off — Pryderi and Rhiannon released, the enchantment lifted from Dyfed, and no vengeance taken for it. The mouse is the wife of Llwyd fab Cilcoed, who had laid the spell to avenge his friend Gwawl fab Clud, the suitor Rhiannon refused. Pryderi comes home with a gate-hammer about his neck, and Rhiannon with the collars of asses about hers; the land wakes, and the Third Branch ends with the four of them feasting as they began. [Fourth Branch · Math fab Mathonwy] The Swine and the Fatal Combat: Among Pryderi's treasures are the hobeu, the first swine ever brought to Wales — a gift to his house from Arawn of Annwn, which Pryderi had sworn neither to sell nor to give until the herd had bred twice its number. Gwydion fab Dôn comes to his court in the guise of a poet, is refused the pigs, and conjures twelve stallions with golden harness, twelve greyhounds with golden collars and leashes, and twelve golden shields — apparitions good for a day and gone by morning — and trades them for the herd. When the glamour fades, Pryderi musters Dyfed and comes north, and the war that follows forces the crime Gwydion and Gilfaethwy commit against Goewin. At the peace-talks Pryderi demands single combat, for it was because of him the hosts had come; at Y Felenrhyd, the tale says, Gwydion slew him 'by strength and valour, and by magic and enchantment'. They buried Pryderi there, at Maen Tywynog above Y Felenrhyd — and his grave, the Fourth Branch says, is there.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Ceridwen".
output: Ceridwen's whole dossier is a single tale — Hanes Taliesin, the Tale of Taliesin — preserved in sixteenth-century Welsh manuscripts and customarily printed with the Mabinogion, though it is none of the Four Branches. Within that tale she owns its great engine: the cauldron, the hunt, and the rebirth. [Hanes Taliesin] The Household by Llyn Tegid: In the beginning, the tale says, Ceridwen lived beside Llyn Tegid in the land of Penllyn, the wife of Tegid Foel — Tegid the Bald — whose name the lake still carries. They had two children whose fortunes were weighed in opposite scales: a daughter, Creirwy, the fairest maiden in the world, and a son, Morfran, so dark and ill-favoured that he was called Afagddu, Utter Darkness. No god could have made the boy handsome; but Ceridwen was skilled in the arts, and she resolved to give him what nature had refused — knowledge and the gift of poetry, so that his birth might yet be honoured among men of culture. [Hanes Taliesin] The Cauldron of a Year and a Day: From the books of the feryllt — the Welsh name for the alchemist's art — Ceridwen compounded a cauldron of Inspiration and Science. It must boil a year and a day, ceaselessly, until three drops of the spirit of inspiration should be won from it. To keep the vigil she set a blind man, Morda, to kindle the fire beneath, and a servant-boy, Gwion Bach, son of Gwreang of Llanfair in Powys, to stir the pot. The design was exact and the patience enormous: everything in the tale that follows is the unmaking of this design by a single splash. [Hanes Taliesin] The Three Drops and the Flight of Shapes: At the year's end the three charmed drops leapt from the cauldron — and fell, not on Morfran, but on the finger of Gwion Bach. The boy put his burning finger in his mouth, and in that instant all the awen was his: he knew all that was past and all that was to come, and knew above all that Ceridwen would kill him. He fled. She pursued; and the pursuit is the oldest Welsh telling of the magic flight, the transformation chase of the folktales. He became a hare; she became a greyhound and gained on him. He leapt into a river and became a fish; she became an otter-bitch behind him. He rose into the air as a bird; she was a hawk on his wing. Every shape he took, she took its hunter. [Hanes Taliesin] The Grain of Wheat and the Black Hen: Spent at last, Gwion dropped into a barn and hid himself as one grain of winnowed wheat on the threshing-floor. Ceridwen became a high-crested black hen, went to the wheat, found the grain, and swallowed it. The swallowing is the tale's hinge: she carried him nine months, and when she bore him again he was so beautiful that she could not do what she had sworn — she could not kill him. So she sewed him in a hide bag and cast him into the sea, to the mercy of God, on the twenty-ninth of April. With that, Ceridwen passes out of her own story; she never appears again. [Hanes Taliesin] The Radiant Brow: The sea carried the bag to the salmon-weir of Gwyddno Garanhir, near the mouth of the Dyfi, and there on May Day Gwyddno's son Elffin found it among the fish. Opening it, he saw the boy's forehead and cried out what became a name: 'Behold the radiant brow' — tal iesin. 'Taliesin be I called,' the child answered, and as Elffin carried him home on horseback the boy sang his first poem, a song of consolation: Fair Elphin, cease your weeping. Years later, when Maelgwn Gwynedd imprisoned Elffin, the boy Taliesin went to the king's court, shamed every bard in the hall with poems they could not match, foretold the king's death, and freed his foster-father. The inspiration Ceridwen brewed for one son had become the making of another: the greatest poet of the Welsh tradition is, in the end, her child — swallowed, carried, born again, and set adrift by her own hands.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Annwn".
output: Annwn is named in the very first pages of the Mabinogi and in the most difficult poem of early Welsh tradition. Its dossier is small and immense: a king who trades his shape, a cauldron that will not boil a coward's food, a hunt that keeps the world's demons leashed — and, behind all three, the deep itself. [Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed (First Branch)] The Year in Annwn: Pwyll, prince of Dyfed, is hunting in Glyn Cuch when he drives a strange pack off a stag — hounds gleaming white, with red ears, the colours of the Otherworld — and feeds his own dogs on the kill. Their master rides up: [[arawn|Arawn]], a king of Annwn, and the offense is real. To make amends Pwyll accepts Arawn's bargain: for a year and a day they will exchange shapes and kingdoms, and at the year's end Pwyll must face Arawn's rival Hafgan — a king who can be killed by a single blow only; strike him twice and by the next day he fights as strongly as before. Pwyll rules Annwn for the year in Arawn's likeness, in a court of unsurpassed plenty — and each night lies beside Arawn's queen without once touching her. At the appointed ford he strikes Hafgan once, refuses the second blow the wounded king begs for, and Annwn is united under Arawn. When the two kings meet again at Glyn Cuch and resume their own shapes, Arawn learns of the year's chastity and the friendship is sealed with gifts of horses, greyhounds, hawks, and gold. From that day Pwyll was called not Pwyll Prince of Dyfed but Pwyll Pen Annwn — Pwyll, Head of Annwn. [Preiddeu Annwfn (Book of Taliesin)] The Spoils of Annwn: The poem Preiddeu Annwfn, 'The Spoils of Annwfn', preserved in the fourteenth-century Book of Taliesin and spoken in the poet's own voice, is the oldest surviving account of an Arthurian Otherworld raid. Arthur sails in his ship Prydwen against the fortresses of the deep — Caer Sidi, Caer Pedryfan, Caer Wydyr, and the rest — and the refrain tolls after each: 'except seven, none returned from Caer Sidi.' Three full loads of Prydwen went into Annwn; seven men came back. The prize is the cauldron of the Head of Annwfn — kindled by the breath of nine maidens, its rim set about with pearls, and marked by the rule the Welsh tradition fixes on Otherworld vessels: it will not boil the food of a coward. The poem is elliptical, proud, and mournful at once — the poet stands apart from the swordsmen who went in and never came out — but its facts became permanent: the Otherworld has a cauldron, Arthur went to get it, and almost no one returned. [Culhwch ac Olwen] Gwyn ap Nudd and the Demons of Annwn: The great hunting catalogue of Culhwch ac Olwen names its most uncanny huntsman: Gwyn ap Nudd, son of Nudd — 'God has set him over the demons of Annwn, lest this world be destroyed.' The hunt of the boar Twrch Trwyth cannot be accomplished without him, and so Gwyn rides out of Annwn at Arthur's muster: the Otherworld's own power, conscripted to keep its worst inhabitants leashed. The same tale gives Gwyn his famous quarrel. He had carried off Creiddylad, daughter of Lludd, from her father's house, and Gwythyr ap Greidawl raised a host and took her back; Arthur judged between them — the maiden to remain with her father, and the two to fight for her every May Day until the Day of Judgment, when the winner takes her for good. Gwyn's hunt is therefore not seasonal sport but a standing order: Annwn's violence rides out under a king who is himself a covenant. [Buchedd Collen] The King on Glastonbury Tor: The Welsh Life of St Collen gives Annwn its most local address. Collen, keeping his hermitage under Glastonbury Tor, hears two men say that Gwyn ap Nudd — king of Annwn and of the Tylwyth Teg, the Fair Folk — holds his court above. Collen answers that the hosts of the air are demons; a summons follows, and on the summit he finds a castle of the utmost splendour, the king on a golden chair, and a banquet of dishes he has never seen the like of. Collen sprinkles his holy water over the food, and the whole vision dissolves — castle, court, and king gone as if they had never been, leaving the saint standing on the green Tor. The tale is late and Christian, but it keeps the old facts in place: Gwyn is king of Annwn, his hall is a feast beyond earthly measure, and the Otherworld can open on a hillside in Somerset and close again without a trace.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Fūjin".
output: Fūjin's mythology is grounded in the creation narratives of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki , in popular Buddhist iconography, and in the visual tradition of Japanese screen painting. He is both a primordial force and a temple guardian. [Kojiki / Nihon Shoki] The Birth of Fūjin: The wind kami are older than the name Fūjin. In the Kojiki 's birth-of-the-kami sequence, Shinatsuhiko-no-mikoto, the wind deity, is born to Izanagi and Izanami among the elemental gods that follow the making of the islands. The Nihon Shoki adds its own etiology: Izanagi blows away the morning mist that wraps the new-made land, and from that breath the wind kami is born. The thunder kami, by contrast, are born from Izanami's corpse after her death in the birth of the fire god — neither wind nor thunder kami are products of Izanagi's later purification at the misogi. The demonic figure called Fūjin — leopard skin, wind-bag, streaming hair — is the later, Buddhist-inflected portrait of these older wind kami. [Nihon Shoki] Wind in the Age of the Gods: The wind kami appear in several episodes of the divine age. When the sun goddess Amaterasu withdrew into the cave, the winds stilled and the world grew dark. When she was lured out, life — including the movement of air — returned. Fūjin thus belongs to the same cosmic order governed by the sun and storm; his winds are part of the vitality that returns when divine harmony is restored. [Buddhist iconography] Guardian of the Four Heavens: In esoteric Buddhism the wind god is Fūten, one of the Twelve Devas ( jūniten ) who guard the directions; protector of the north-west, he adapts the Indian wind god Vāyu transmitted through the mandalas of esoteric ritual. He protects the Dharma by sweeping away obstacles and evil influences. Temples across Japan, including Sanjūsangen-dō in Kyōto and the Kennin-ji in Kyōto, house famous depictions of Fūjin and Raijin as muscular, wind-whipped guardians.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Kanaloa".
output: Hawaiian myths present Kānāloa as a complementary power to Kāne, the creator. Their partnership structures much of traditional cosmology. [Creation] Kāne and Kānāloa: In Hawaiian cosmogony, Kāne and Kānāloa are paired creator gods. Together they travel across the primordial ocean, striking the earth with their staffs to create springs and bring forth life. Kāne is the fresh water and the sunlight; Kānāloa is the salt sea that surrounds and sustains the islands. Their partnership is not hierarchy but dynamic balance. [Healing] The Discovery of Medicine: Kānāloa fell ill, and no remedy could be found. Kāne prayed and was shown the healing plants of the forest and shore. After Kānāloa was cured, the two gods shared this knowledge with humankind, establishing the practice of lāʻau lapaʻau, traditional Hawaiian herbal medicine. Illness and cure both belong to Kānāloa's watery realm. [Underworld] The Dark Realm: Kānāloa is also the lord of the underworld, the realm beneath the earth and sea where souls journey after death. Unlike the Christian hell, this realm is not primarily punitive; it is the mysterious mirror of the living world, governed by the same god whose waters feed the land above.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Ītzpāpālōtl".
output: Itzpapālōtl belongs to the dangerous borderlands: between paradise and underworld, birth and death, daylight and eclipse. Her myths are preserved in fragments of the Florentine Codex and Borgia group codices. [Origin] The Lady of Tamoanchan: Tamoanchan is the mythical paradise of origins, a lush mountain of flowers and fruit where the creator couple dwelt. Itzpapālōtl rules there as both guardian and destroyer, her obsidian wings protecting the tree from which the first humans were fashioned. To approach her is to risk being flayed by the very beauty one admires. [Childbirth] The Cihuateteo: Women who died in childbirth were not ordinary dead. They became Cihuateteo, 'divine women', fierce spirits who accompanied the sun from zenith to sunset and prowled crossroads at night. Itzpapālōtl is their mother and queen. Because they had died bringing life, they had power over both: they could bless children or steal them away. instruction: Tell me a myth about "Tàijí".
output: Tàijí has no body and no biography; its 'mythology' is the story Chinese thinkers told about how the one becomes many. The most influential telling is Zhou Dunyi's short prose poem, but it draws on much older Daoist and Yijing material. [Zhou Dunyi, Taijitu shuo] Wújí ér Tàijí: Zhou Dunyi's Explanation of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate opens: 'Wújí ér Tàijí' — the limitless, and yet the supreme ultimate. From this arise movement and stillness, yang and yin, the five phases, and finally the moral order of the sage. The text became the cosmological charter of Song Neo-Confucianism and shaped Chinese state orthodoxy for centuries. [Daodejing] The Dao Gives Birth to One: Laozi describes a parallel cosmogony in Daodejing 42: 'The Dao gives birth to one; one gives birth to two; two gives birth to three; three gives birth to the ten thousand things.' The 'one' has often been read as Tàijí, the primordial unity that precedes the duality of yin and yang. [Yijing] The Great Treatise: The Xici appendices of the Yijing declare that 'in change there is Tàijí; Tàijí gives birth to the two modes.' Here Tàijí is not merely a Neo-Confucian innovation but the philosophical root of the book of divination, the still point from which all hexagrams unfold. [Martial Legend] Zhang Sanfeng and the Birth of Taijiquan: Daoist tradition credits the semi-legendary Zhang Sanfeng with founding Taijiquan after watching a snake and crane fight on Wudang Mountain. The story is probably apocryphal, but it captures the art's core insight: victory comes from yielding, centering, and following the opponent's force rather than meeting it.

Modern Standard Mandarin (Pinyin) Note: 五行 (Wǔxíng) denotes the 'Five Phases' or 'Five Agents'—wood, fire, earth, metal, and water—the cyclical modes of transformation in Chinese cosmology, medicine, and feng shui. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading in this philosophical context is wǔ (Tone 3) + xíng (Tone 2), as given by the Unihan Database (kMandarin) and the Hanyu Pinyin scheme. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct 五 as *C.ŋˤaʔ (GSR 0058a) and 行 in the sense 'walk, conduct' as *C.[g]raŋ (GSR 0748a). instruction: Tell me a myth about "Váli".
output: Váli appears briefly but decisively in the Norse corpus. His myths are episodes in the larger tragedy of Baldr and the doom of the gods. [Völuspá] Born for Vengeance: After Baldr is slain, the gods cannot simply kill Höðr, for he is one of their own and acted in blindness. Óðinn therefore fathers Váli on Rindr, a reluctant giantess. Váli grows to full strength in a single day, takes up his bow, and slays Höðr in the holy place. The killing is ritually necessary and morally ambiguous: it rights one wrong with another. [Prose Edda] The Binding of Loki: When Loki flees Asgard after engineering Baldr's death, the gods capture him in a riverside house. They seize his sons Váli and Nari (or Narfi): Váli is turned into a wolf and tears his own brother Nari apart, and the Æsir bind Loki with Nari's entrails to three stones beneath the earth (Gylfaginning 50). This wolf-Váli is Loki's son, not Óðinn's; Óðinn's Váli plays no part in the binding. A snake drips venom on Loki's face until Ragnarök, when he will break free and steer the ship of the dead against the gods. [Eschatology] After Ragnarök: Most of the gods perish in the final battle, but Váli is among the survivors. Together with Víðarr, Baldr, and Höðr (returned from Hel), he inhabits the renewed world that rises from the flood. His function—vengeance—has been fulfilled; what remains is the quiet inheritance of a world without Loki's malice.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Hati".
output: Hati's mythology is a single image carried by a handful of verses: a wolf, a moon, and a chase that ends only with the world. The Poetic Edda names him once, Snorri gives him his quarry and his ending, and Völuspá's seeress supplies the brood he springs from. [Grímnismál 39] The Pair Before Heaven: The name's one poetic attestation comes in Óðinn's great catalogue of the cosmos in Grímnismál, where the disguised god enumerates the heavens for the torture-bound Geirrøðr: 'Skǫll is the name of the wolf who follows the bright-faced god to the sheltering wood; but the other is Hati, Hróðvitnir's son, who runs before the bright bride of heaven.' The bright bride of heaven is the sun; the wolf who runs before her is on the heels of the moon, which travels ahead of her. In four lines the Edda converts the machinery of the sky into a hunt: what astronomy calls a course, the poem calls a chase. [Gylfaginning 12] Skǫll After the Sun, Hati After the Moon: Snorri systematizes the verse. When Gangleri asks why the sun hurries so — 'she speeds as if she were afraid' — High One answers that she has good cause: 'the one who seeks her is right behind her, and she has no other way out than to run.' Two wolves do the work of the heavens: Skǫll chases the sun and will catch her, and 'the other wolf is called Hati Hróðvitnisson; he runs in front of her and wants to catch the moon — and that is what will happen.' Snorri's gloss fixes the reading the poem left compressed, and with it the moon's doom is put on the schedule of things foretold. [Gylfaginning 12] Mánagarmr, the Moon-Hound: In the same chapter Snorri names the mightiest of the wolf-brood: Mánagarmr, 'moon-hound' — 'he will be filled with the flesh of all who die, and he will swallow the moon and spatter the sky and all the air with blood; from this the sun will lose its brightness.' Whether Mánagarmr is Hati under a second name or a third wolf beside the pair, the manuscripts and the handbooks leave open; Simek and Lindow record the identification as probable but unprovable. What is certain is the image: the moon taken, and the blood of the swallowed light staining heaven. [Völuspá 39-40] The Brood of the Ironwood: Völuspá's seeress supplies the kennel. 'In the east sat the old one in the Ironwood and bred there Fenrir's brood; from all of them comes one in particular, a snatcher of the moon in a troll's skin. He gorges on the life of doomed men, reddens the gods' dwellings with red blood; the sunshine turns black in the summers after, and all weathers run hostile.' The poem names no name — but the tungls tjúgari, the 'snatcher of the moon', is the role Grímnismál and Snorri assign to Hati, and the handbooks read the figures together: the Ironwood breeds the chase, and the chase ends the world. [Gylfaginning 51 · Völuspá] The Catch at Ragnarǫk: The ending is shared by every witness. When Ragnarǫk comes, the wolves' running stops: Skǫll takes the sun, Hati takes the moon, Fenrir himself swallows Óðinn, and 'the sun turns black, earth sinks into the sea, the bright stars vanish from the sky.' The Edda's cosmology is built so that the nightly order of the heavens is only an interval — the long meanwhile between the start of the chase and its foreknown end. Hati never fails of his quarry; he simply has not caught it yet.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Manawydan".
output: Manawydan's dossier is the Second and Third Branches of the Mabinogi: Branwen ferch Llŷr, where he is one of the seven who bring the head home, and Manawydan fab Llŷr, the branch that bears his name — the quietest and most perfectly built of the Four, a tale in which an entire kingdom is stolen by silence and won back by patience. [Second Branch · Branwen ferch Llŷr] The Seven Who Brought the Head Home: Manawydan stands beside his brother Brân — Bendigeidfran, the Blessed — when [[matholwch|Matholwch]], king of Ireland, comes to Harlech to ask for their sister Branwen, and he counsels the marriage that begins the whole catastrophe. When the insult of the mutilated horses has festered into war, Brân wades the sea to Ireland, and the host that crosses with him comes home as seven men: Pryderi, Manawydan, Glifieu Eil Taran, [[taliesin|Taliesin]], Ynawg, Gruddieu fab Muriel, and Heilyn fab Gwyn — bearing the head of Brân, struck by a poisoned spear, which talks with them and is better company than ever it was in life. At Harlech they feast seven years with the head, the three songs of the birds of Rhiannon singing to them, and time does not move. At Gwales in Penfro they find a royal hall with two doors open and one shut — toward Cornwall — and there they pass eighty years in the Assembly of the Wondrous Head, forgetting every sorrow, until Heilyn fab Gwyn says 'shame on my beard if I do not open the door' — and opens it, and all their losses come back at once like a tide. Then they do as the head had commanded: they carry it to London and bury it in the White Mount, facing France, and the triads count that burial among the Three Fortunate Concealments of the Island of Britain. Manawydan, who had counseled the wedding, survives its end — the pattern of his whole life in one branch. [Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr] The Counsel and the Marriage: While Brân's host was in Ireland, Caswallawn fab [[beli|Beli]] — Manawydan's own cousin — had struck down the men left in charge and taken the crown of London. Pryderi, lord of Dyfed and son of Pwyll and [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]], would have fought him; Manawydan counsels otherwise: Caswallawn is their kinsman, and the kingdom has suffered enough of war. It is the most characteristic speech in the whole Mabinogi — a man with the best claim to vengeance declining it out of arithmetic and mercy. Pryderi yields, and gives Manawydan the fairest compensation the tale can imagine: his mother's hand and the seven cantrefs of Dyfed. Manawydan and Rhiannon wed, and the four — Manawydan, Rhiannon, Pryderi, and Pryderi's wife Cigfa — live at Arberth in unbroken fellowship. [Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr] The Thunder and the Mist: They go up Gorsedd Arberth, the mound where, in the First Branch, wonders came to Pwyll — and wonder comes. As they sit, a peal of thunder falls, and with it a mist so thick they cannot see one another. When it lifts, Dyfed is gone: no dwelling, no animal, no smoke, no man, no woman — only the four of them and the empty land, house and court and courtiers vanished together. For a year they live by hunting and the kindness of the emptied land; for a second year they bear it; in the third they grow weary of it, and the tale turns from endurance to answer. [Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr] The White Boar and the Golden Bowl: Hunting, Pryderi and Manawydan rouse a boar shining white, which leads their dogs to a fortress neither has ever seen — and no one ever sees twice. Against Manawydan's counsel Pryderi goes in after the dogs and finds a fountain with a marble slab, and on the slab a golden bowl fastened by chains, wrought with a craftsmanship he cannot fathom. He reaches for it: his hands stick to the bowl, his feet to the slab, and speech leaves him. Rhiannon, hearing her son lost, reproaches Manawydan for returning without him, goes in, lays hold of the bowl, and is taken the same way — and with thunder and a fall of mist the fortress vanishes with them both. Manawydan is left with Cigfa, and the branch's second act belongs to them alone. [Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr] The Three Crafts of Hereford: Manawydan will not beg his bread in an emptied kingdom: 'Let us go into Lloegr,' he tells Cigfa, 'and take up a craft.' At Hereford he becomes a saddler, and his saddles are so fine that Hereford's saddlers, losing every customer, conspire to kill the strangers; Pryderi's heir would fight, Manawydan counts the odds, and they move on. He becomes a shield-maker — the same beauty, the same conspiracy, the same dignified retreat. He becomes a shoemaker, gilding the shoes, and the cordwainers drive them out like the rest. Three trades, each mastered at first attempt, each surrendered rather than repaid in blood: the triads never forgot it, ranking Manawydan among the Three Golden Shoemakers of the Island of Britain. [Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr] The Trial of the Mouse: Back in empty Dyfed, Manawydan sows three crofts of wheat, and they come up the finest in the land. The first croft, ripe for reaping, is found in the morning stripped to the bare straw; the second goes the same way. On the third night Manawydan keeps watch, and sees a host of mice descend on the ears, each mouse stripping an ear and carrying it off. He runs them down and catches one — the fattest, and slow, and heavy with young. He sets a miniature gallows on the gorsedd and condemns her as a thief. Then the ransomers come: a scholar, then a priest, then a bishop, each more richly robed than the last, each offering money for the felon's life, and to each Manawydan answers that he will not sell a convicted thief — until the bishop, pressed to name his terms, hears them whole: Pryderi and Rhiannon freed, the enchantment lifted from Dyfed, no vengeance taken on the mice, and no spell ever laid on the seven cantrefs again. The bishop is Llwyd fab Cil Coed, enchanter and friend of Gwawl fab Clud — Rhiannon's jilted suitor from the First Branch — and the whole desolation was his long revenge; the mice were his own household and warband under shape, and the fat one his wife. Pryderi comes back with the gate-hammers he had been made to carry, Rhiannon with the collars of asses about her neck, the mist lifts from Dyfed, and Manawydan keeps his word to the letter: not one mouse is harmed. It is the Mabinogi's most complete victory, and no sword is drawn in it.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Blodeuwedd".
output: Blodeuwedd exists in exactly one witness, and it is enough: the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi, 'Math uab Mathonwy', the masterpiece of medieval Welsh prose. She enters the tale as its most beautiful artefact and leaves it as its most haunting sentence — a woman made from flowers, a bride who chose her own lover, and an owl that still bears her name in modern Welsh. [Math fab Mathonwy] Made of Flowers: When Arianrhod, shamed by the birth the wand had forced from her, laid her third destiny on her son — that he should never have a wife of any race then on earth — Math the king took counsel with [[gwydion|Gwydion]]: 'Let us try, by charms and enchantment, to conjure a wife for him out of flowers.' They took the flowers of the oak, the flowers of the broom, and the flowers of the meadowsweet, and from them made the fairest and most beautiful woman anyone had ever seen; they baptized her in the manner of the time, and named her Blodeuwedd, Flower-face. The wedding sealed the counter-spell: Lleu was given the cantref of Dinoding to rule, and the pair settled at his court in Ardudwy, at the place called Mur Castell. The Fourth Branch gives the marriage one sentence of happiness — everyone was content — before it sets the trap the whole tale has been building toward: a king's nephew with a destiny, and a wife who was never born of woman at all. [Math fab Mathonwy] Gronw of Penllyn: Lleu went to Caer Dathyl to visit Math, and while he was away Gronw Pebr, the lord of Penllyn, came hunting into the country. At nightfall Blodeuwedd welcomed the hunter into the court — the hospitality owed to a guest — and the tale says simply that that night they talked, and she conceived a love for him, and he for her. Three nights they lay together while her husband sat at his uncle's court. The Fourth Branch wastes no breath condemning them; it reports desire with the same flat care it gives to flower-making. But the lovers' question is the tale's hinge: how can they be together for good? Blodeuwedd's answer is to learn what only a wife can learn — the manner of her husband's death — and the text lets her do it in his own trust, 'in the guise of concern', asking how a man so strangely fated could ever be killed. [Math fab Mathonwy] The Impossible Conditions: Lleu, trusting, told her everything. He cannot be killed indoors or out of doors, on horseback or on foot. He can be killed only in one posture: a bath prepared on the bank of a river, a thatched frame over the tub, one foot on the rim of the cauldron and the other on the back of a billy-goat — and only by a spear worked for a full year, and only during the hours of Mass on Sundays. Blodeuwedd sent every word to Gronw, and Gronw set the smiths to work. When the year was out she asked her husband to show her the marvellous stance — she would never understand it, she said, unless she saw it. The bath was drawn, the frame thatched, the goat brought; Lleu set one foot on the cauldron's rim and one on the goat, and Gronw rose from the hill called Bryn Cyfergyr and cast the spear. It struck Lleu in the side so the shaft stood out of him and the head stayed in, and with a terrible scream he flew up in the shape of an eagle and was gone. Gronw took the lands, and the flower-bride's making came to its harvest. [Math fab Mathonwy] The Lake of the Maidens: When Math and Gwydion came against Gronw, Blodeuwedd heard of it and fled with her maidens into the mountains. But fear made them walk backward, looking always behind them for the pursuit, until the whole company walked into a lake and drowned — all of them except Blodeuwedd herself. The tale names the place for them: Llyn y Morwynion, the Lake of the Maidens. Gwydion overtook her in the mountains and took her. The image the Fourth Branch leaves is among the coldest in Welsh literature: the made woman fleeing through the dark with her dead companions behind her under the water, caught at last not by a warrior but by the enchanter who had fashioned her out of blossoms three years — or one lifetime — before. [Math fab Mathonwy] The Owl's Sentence: Gwydion's judgement is the Fourth Branch's second great transformation-sentence, and it is precise: 'I will not kill you; I will do what is worse. I will let you go in the shape of a bird. Because of the dishonour you have done Lleu Llaw Gyffes, you shall never dare show your face in the light of day, and that shall be from fear of all birds: they shall mob you and molest you wherever they find you. And you shall not lose your name, but shall always be called Blodeuwedd.' She went, in the shape of the owl. The tale adds its own etiology: blodeuwedd is what the owl is called to this day, and for that reason the birds hate the owl wherever it is found. The aftermath belongs to the slain man's healing and the standing stone: Lleu, nursed back from eagle-shape and skin and bone, demanded to stand where Gronw had stood; Gronw took the stone slab between himself and the spear, and Lleu's cast drove through the slab and through him. The pierced stone on the bank of the Cynfael was called Llech Ronw, Gronw's stone. Blodeuwedd alone of the tale's dead is not buried — she is still flying, under her flower-name, in every Welsh word for owl.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Math".
output: Math fab Mathonwy is the king at the still centre of the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi — the branch that bears his name: lord of Gwynedd, master of the magic wand, uncle of Gwydion and Gilfaethwy. His rule hangs on the strangest condition in Welsh literature — he cannot live except with his feet in a virgin's lap, unless war calls him out — and around that geas the whole plot turns: the theft of the swine, the wrong to Goewin, the justice of the three animal years, and the making of a bride from flowers. [Math fab Mathonwy] The Geas of the Footholder: Math son of Mathonwy was lord over Gwynedd, and the tale's first fact about him is the condition of his life: except when the turmoil of war prevented it, he could not live unless his feet lay in the lap of a virgin. The office of footholder went to Goewin daughter of Pebin of Dôl Pebin in Arfon, the fairest maiden of her generation; and while Math kept the lap, his sister's sons Gwydion and Gilfaethwy ruled the realm in his stead. The arrangement is neither joke nor luxury: it is the Fourth Branch's picture of sacral kingship, a rule whose life is bound by taboo. When Gilfaethwy sickened with desire for Goewin, Gwydion read the geas like a statute. The king may leave the lap for one thing only — war. Therefore there would be a war. [Math fab Mathonwy] The War for the Swine: Pryderi of Dyfed held the hobeu, the swine sent him from Annwfn by its king Arawn — the first pigs ever brought to Wales. Gwydion went south in the guise of a poet, conjured twelve stallions with golden harness, twelve greyhounds with golden collars, and twelve golden shields, traded the day's glamour for the herd, and was gone before the illusion faded. Pryderi mustered and came north, and Math led Gwynedd out to meet him — out of the lap, exactly as the condition required. At the parley Pryderi demanded single combat, for it was because of him that the hosts had come; at the maenor of Penardd Gwydion slew him 'by strength and valour and by magic and enchantment', and Dyfed gave hostages and went home under tribute. But while Math marched, Gwydion and Gilfaethwy forced Goewin in the king's own chamber. The war had only ever been the key, and the lap the lock. [Math fab Mathonwy] The Queen and the Three Skins: Goewin would not hide what had been done to her, and Math's first act was redress: he took her as his wife and made her queen, so that the disgrace should not fall on her. Then came judgment. He struck Gwydion and Gilfaethwy with his magic wand into a stag and a hind, and sent them into the wild for a year; when they returned with a fawn, he made them a boar and a sow for the second year, and a wolf and a she-wolf for the third. Each year's offspring — Hyddwn, Hychddwn Hir, and Bleiddwn — the king took in beast-shape, restored to human form, baptized, and raised. After the third year he struck the brothers back into men: they had had punishment enough, he said, and been greatly shamed, and he received them back into honour. It is the most exact justice in the Mabinogi — transformation as sentence, a year for each skin of the debt, and restoration without residue. [Math fab Mathonwy] The Stepping over the Wand: A new footholder was needed, and Gwydion named his own sister, Arianrhod daughter of Dôn. Math put the question plainly — was she a virgin? — and set the test: step over my wand. As she stepped, she dropped a sturdy yellow-haired boy. Math had him baptized at once and named him Dylan, and the boy made straight for the sea and took its nature, Dylan son of Wave. And as Arianrhod turned to go, she dropped 'something small', which Gwydion swept up and hid in a chest at the foot of his bed — the boy who would be Lleu Llaw Gyffes. The wand that punishes is also the wand that proves: in one gesture the age of footholders ended and the age of the Children of Dôn began. [Math fab Mathonwy] The Bride Made of Flowers: Arianrhod, shamed before the court, laid her tynghedau on the boy: he should have no name until she named him, no arms until she armed him, and no wife of any race then on earth. Gwydion's craft undid the first two; for the third there was no earthly answer, and it was Math who joined him in making one. The two enchanters took their wands and, from the flowers of the oak, the broom, and the meadowsweet, fashioned the fairest and most beautiful maiden anyone had seen, baptized her, and named her Blodeuwedd — and gave her to Lleu. The tale records no death for Math. The branch ends with Lleu restored and avenged, ruling Gwynedd after, and the old king simply withdraws from the record — the stillness at the centre to the last.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Śākyamuni".
output: The life of Śākyamuni is the best-attested sacred biography of the ancient world — told in the Pāli Nikāyas, versified by Aśvaghoṣa, expanded in the Nidānakathā and the Lalitavistara, and anchored in the ground by Aśoka's own inscriptions. [Nidānakathā / Lalitavistara] The Birth at Lumbinī: Queen Māyā, traveling to her father's house, gave birth standing in the grove at Lumbinī, holding the branch of a sāla tree; the child took seven steps and declared this his last birth. The legends multiplied — the shower of blossoms, the two streams of water, the prophecy of the sage Asita — but the place is fixed in stone: Aśoka's pillar at Rummindei, raised in his twentieth regnal year, reads in plain Prakrit, hida budhe jāte sakyamuni — "here the Buddha Śākyamuni was born." It is the only birthplace of a world teacher certified by a contemporary emperor. [Ariyapariyesanā Sutta] The Four Sights and the Going Forth: Sheltered in three palaces, the young Śākyan saw what his father had fenced out: an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering ascetic — the four sights the later tradition makes the hinge of his life. In the Majjhima Nikāya's Ariyapariyesanā Sutta (MN 26) he tells it himself: he shaved his hair, put on the ochre robe, and went forth from home into homelessness while still young, in the prime of life, with his parents weeping. The great renunciation — the night ride on Kaṇṭhaka with the groom Channa — became Buddhist art's first epic scene. [SN 56.11] The Awakening and the First Turning: Six years of austerities on the Nairañjanā brought him to the edge of death and the discovery of the middle way; seated under the Bodhi tree at Uruvelā he withstood Māra's assault, touched the earth as his witness, and by dawn saw the four noble truths and the chain of dependent arising. Weeks later, in the deer park at Ṛṣipatana near Benares — Sarnath — he taught the five ascetics the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (SN 56.11), the setting-in-motion of the wheel: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the eightfold path. The sermon is preserved in every Buddhist canon; the wheel he turned has not stopped. [Mahāparinibbāna Sutta] The Last Days at Kusinārā: The Dīgha Nikāya's Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (DN 16) follows his last journey with a chronicler's eye: the meal offered by the smith Cunda, the sickness, the couch laid northward between twin sāla trees in the Mallas' grove at Kusinārā, which burst into blossom out of season. His last instruction was a refusal of permanence itself: "All conditioned things are of a nature to decay — strive on with diligence." The Mallas cremated him as a universal monarch, and his relics were divided into eight shares and enshrined in stupas — the beginning of Buddhist sacred architecture.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Māra".
output: Māra's mythology is the dark half of the Buddhist biography: wherever the teaching advances, the texts station him at the next bend — and his defeats chart the whole path from striving to parinibbāna. [Padhāna Sutta (Sn 3.2)] The Ten Armies: The Sutta Nipāta's Padhāna Sutta gives his order of battle, and it is a psychology textbook in disguise: sensual pleasure is his first army, discontent the second, hunger and thirst the third, craving the fourth, sloth and torpor the fifth, fear the sixth, doubt the seventh, hypocrisy and obstinacy the eighth, gains, fame, and honor the ninth, and the tenth is self-exaltation joined with contempt for others. The Buddha's answer is the template of every later victory: he sees each army for what it is. The tradition's whole art of temptation is this catalog — and its whole defense is recognition. [Nidānakathā / Buddhacarita] The Night Under the Tree: The full assault is told in the Nidānakathā and versified in Aśvaghoṣa's Buddhacarita, whose canto on the Defeat of Māra is Sanskrit poetry's great set-piece: whirlwinds that cannot stir his robe, a rain of rocks that falls as flowers, darkness that will not spread. Mounted on the elephant Girimekhala, Māra advances his final claim — the seat of awakening is his — and calls his army as witness. The bodhisattva answers with the gesture that defines Buddhist art: he touches the earth, and the earth itself thunders witness to his perfections. The elephant kneels; the army scatters; the dawn comes up on an undefeated man. [Māradhītu Sutta (SN 4.25)] The Daughters: Force having failed, Māra sent subtlety: his three daughters, Taṇhā (Craving), Aratī (Aversion), and Rāgā (Passion), came to the newly-awakened Buddha in every guise of beauty and made their offer. He saw through each in turn, and dismissed them with the calm of a man reading names off a list. The Saṃyutta Nikāya's Māra cycle ends nearly every one of these duels the same way — with the Tempter's signature lament: "The Blessed One knows me; the Fortunate One knows me." It is the most repeated sentence of defeat in any scripture: to be seen is to be beaten. [Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (DN 16)] The Last Visit: Māra keeps one appointment to the end. In the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta he comes to the aged Buddha and, with perfect courtesy, reminds him of his ancient promise: that he would not pass away until the four assemblies — monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen — were well established. That work is done now; it is time for the Blessed One's parinibbāna. And the Buddha, who once broke his army by seeing him, grants the request without resistance: in three months the Tathāgata will pass away. The tradition's point is exact — the tempter's last success is only the world's impermanence keeping its schedule.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "ꜥAnat".
output: ꜥAnat's mythology is preserved chiefly in the Ugaritic Baꜥal Cycle and the Epic of Aqhat. She is not a fertility goddess in the usual sense; she is force itself, concentrated in a young woman's body, and her stories turn on violence, loyalty, and the refusal to accept limits. [The Baal Cycle] Wading in Blood: In KTU 1.3 ii, ꜥAnat returns from battle in exultation: 'Heads rolled beneath her like balls, hands flew over her like locusts.' She fastens severed heads to her back and hands to her belt, then washes herself clean in the dew sent by Baꜥal, the Rider on the Clouds. The scene is shocking not because she is evil but because she is unrestrained — war as ecstasy, not duty. [The Baal Cycle] Avenger of Baꜥal: When Mot, Death, swallows Baꜥal and the rains fail, ꜥAnat searches the wilderness for her brother. Finding Mot, she attacks him with a sword, winnows him like grain, burns him, grinds him, and scatters him in a field (KTU 1.6 ii 30–35). Her violence is the engine of Baꜥal's return and the renewal of fertility. [Epic of Aqhat] The Bow of the Hero: In KTU 1.17–19, the craftsman god Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs gives the hero Aqhat a marvelous bow. ꜥAnat covets it and offers Aqhat life without death in exchange; he refuses, telling her that womenfolk do not hunt. Enraged, she has the Sutean warrior Yatpan murder Aqhat. The bow is broken, the land withers, and Aqhat's sister Pughat eventually avenges him. [Hymn] Mistress of the Highlands: A hymn to Anat (KTU 1.13) praises her as a swift huntress and protector of the king. She is invoked as a divine patron of royalty and warfare, her energy channeled from chaotic fury into guardian power.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Mūt".
output: Mōt's mythology is the dark season of the year made personal. His stories are preserved in the Baꜥal Cycle, where he confronts Baꜥal, kills him, and is in turn destroyed and reborn in a cycle that explains drought, death, and the return of fertility. [The Baal Cycle] The Summons: In KTU 1.4 vii–viii, Mōt sends word to Baꜥal: because he was not invited to the storm-god's feast, he will feast on Baꜥal himself. His messengers describe a throat like a lion's, a gullet like a whale's, and an appetite that devours by the double handful. Baꜥal's own envoys are warned not to come too close, 'lest he make you like a lamb in his mouth' (KTU 1.4 viii 17–20). [The Baal Cycle] The Descent and Death: In KTU 1.5, Baꜥal submits. He descends into Mōt's mouth and dies. Ēl mourns on the ground, cutting himself with stones; the rains fail and the earth grows dry. Even the high god cannot reverse Mōt's claim — at least, not directly. The cosmos enters the season of death. [The Baal Cycle] Anat's Harvest: In KTU 1.6 ii, ꜥAnat searches for Baꜥal, buries him on Mount Zaphon, then confronts Mōt. She seizes him, splits him with a sword, winnows him like grain, burns him with fire, grinds him under a millstone, and scatters him over a field. The act is agricultural as much as martial: death itself is threshed, ground, and sown away so that Baꜥal may return. [The Baal Cycle] The Rematch: Seven years later Mōt returns (KTU 1.6 vi). He and Baꜥal fight like bulls, serpents, and stallions, neither able to prevail. Finally the sun-goddess Shapash warns Mōt that Ēl will overturn his throne if he does not yield. Mōt submits, and Baꜥal's kingship is restored. The cycle is not a once-for-all victory but the turning of the seasons: death returns, and is pushed back again.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Šāpšu".
output: Šāpshu's mythology is woven through the Baal Cycle and Ugaritic ritual texts. She does not fight like Anat or Baal; she illuminates, witnesses, and transmits divine will. Her descent into the underworld marks the boundary between day and night, life and death. Her nightly journey links her to the Mesopotamian sun god Shamash and the Greek Helios, though she remains distinctively Levantine and female. [Hymn] Šāpshu the Judge: A Ugaritic hymn invokes Šāpshu as the one who judges the case of the widow, the orphan, and the poor. Like the Babylonian Shamash, she is a divine guarantor of social justice because her light exposes wrongdoing. Kings and litigants alike are called to swear by her, knowing that she sees all.

output: Uppsala means: Upper halls. Domain: Temple, Freyr, Sacred Grove. Pantheon: norse.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Uppsala".
output: Uppsala's dossier is not a god's biography but a sanctuary's record — and it is the fullest any Norse holy place receives. Adam of Bremen describes the temple and its rites from the testimony of the Danish court a generation before the old religion died in Sweden; Snorri gives the site its founding god and its dynasty; the saga of Hrólfr kraki sets a famous treasure-flight on the plain below it. Between the four witnesses, the Upper Halls emerge as the one place where the whole northern religion can be watched at prayer. [Adam of Bremen 4.26] The Golden Temple: Adam of Bremen, archbishop's scholar at Hamburg-Bremen, sets down about 1075 the most exact account of Norse cult that survives. Near Sigtuna, he writes, stands a famous temple called Ubsola, entirely decked with gold, and in it the people worship the statues of three gods: the most powerful, Thor, occupies the throne in the middle of the hall; on either side stand Wodan and Fricco. Thor, Adam explains, governs the air, thunder, lightning, winds, rains, fair weather and crops, and holds his sceptre like Jove; Wodan, 'that is, Frenzy', rules war and gives men strength against enemies, carved in the likeness of an armed man as Mars is shown; Fricco, bestower of peace and pleasure on mortals, is shaped with an immense phallus. Each god has his priests, and the people's vows follow need: in plague or famine they sacrifice to Thor, for war to Wodan, for weddings to Fricco. Adam worked from the reports of the Danish king Sven Estridsen, 'who retained all these facts in his memory', and the scholia added to the text fill in further colour — the temple ringed by a golden chain hanging from the gable, the feasting within. What the account gives the record is irreplaceable: a working temple of the Æsir described in its last generation, by a churchman who wanted it abolished and could not help seeing it clearly. [Adam of Bremen 4.27] The Nine-Day Sacrifice: Adam's second chapter on the site records the great communal rite. It is customary, he writes, to hold a solemn assembly of all the provinces of Sweden at Uppsala every nine years, from which no one may purchase exemption; every man sends his offerings. The sacrifice is of this kind: of every living creature that is male, nine head are offered, by whose blood it is the custom to placate the gods. The bodies are hung in a grove adjoining the temple, a grove so sacred to the heathens that each tree is believed divine because of the death and putrefaction of the victims. Dogs and horses hang there with the men, and one of the Christians told Adam he had seen seventy-two bodies hanging together. The incantations sung at the rite, Adam adds, are so disgraceful that it is better to say nothing of them. A scholion adds the spring beside the temple in which a living man was drowned; if he was not found again, the people's wish would be granted. Every element — the nine-year cycle, the nine of each kind, the grove, the hanging — belongs to the deep grammar of Germanic sacrifice: Thietmar of Merseburg records a parallel nine-year rite at Lejre in Denmark, and Tacitus had described the sacred groves of the continental Germans a thousand years before. Uppsala is where that grammar has its fullest surviving page. [Heimskringla, Ynglingasaga 10] Freyr's Temple and the Uppsala Wealth: Snorri gives the site its founding god. When [[freyr|Freyr]] took the kingdom after his father [[njord|Njörðr]], he built a great temple at Uppsalir, made it his chief seat, and endowed it with all his revenues — lands, livestock, and money: the origin of the Uppsala auðr, the 'Uppsala wealth', the crown estate of the Swedish kings. In his days began the peace and good seasons the Swedes remembered as the best of times, and they credited them to their king; Freyr was worshipped more than other gods because the people grew richer in his peace. His other name was Yngvi, and from him the royal house of the Swedes took its name — the Ynglings, whom the skalds served for centuries after. When Freyr died, the chapter continues, his men would not let the news out. They raised a great mound for him with a door and three holes, and told the Swedes he lived on; for three years gold, silver, and copper were poured through the holes as the people's offerings, while the peace held. When at last the truth came out, the Swedes would not burn him, believing he had brought the good seasons — so the god of the temple lies in a royal mound on his own ground, and the cult and the kingship are one estate. Every detail is euhemerized, and the archaeology keeps answering it: the three great barrows beside the church at Gamla Uppsala are real cremation graves of real sixth- and seventh-century kings. [Skáldskaparmál / Hrólfs saga kraka] Kraki's Seed on the Fyrisvellir: The plain below the Upper Halls has its own legend of gold. Snorri, explaining in Skáldskaparmál why gold may be called 'Kraki's seed', tells of King Aðils at Uppsala and his guest turned rival, Hrólfr kraki of the Danes. When Hrólfr fled Uppsala with treasure taken from Aðils, the Swedish king rode in pursuit with his army; and Hrólfr, seeing the pursuit gain, sowed the stolen gold along the Fyrisvellir, the plain of the river Fyris, so that the Swedes, greedy for the shining harvest, stopped to gather it and let the Danes escape. Aðils himself is said to have stooped from his horse to pick up the ring Svíagriss, 'the pig of the Swedes' — and Hrólfr, watching him grovel for gold, declared he had now bent low the mightiest man in Sweden. The saga tradition keeps Aðils at Uppsala for the rest of his strange life — the king who married his own daughter Yrsa, who sacrificed to a 'dis' and was thrown from his horse in the hall — and the same dynasty rides through Beowulf, where Eadgils son of Ohthere is king of the Scylfings, the 'shieldings' of Sweden. The identification of Beowulf's Swedish royal house with the kings of the Uppsala mounds is one of the oldest convictions of northern scholarship: the poems knew the Upper Halls as the house where kings, gold, and gods were one inheritance.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Midir".
output: Midir's mythology is a single long courtship told in two lifetimes — the fullest Otherworld dossier in the Irish corpus, preserved entire in Tochmarc Étaíne. It begins with a sloe-thorn and a bride-price, passes through jealousy and transformation and a rebirth eleven hundred years later, and ends at a fidchell board in Tara and a war of spades against the hollow hills. Around that spine the tradition adds the fosterage: the lord of Brí Léith reared [[aengus|Óengus]], the Dagda's son, and the tie between the two mounds frames both gods' tales. [Tochmarc Étaíne] The Sloe and the Bride-Price: Midir of Brí Léith was the foster-father of Óengus, and he came to Brú na Bóinne to visit his fosterling. While the boys of the Brug were at their hurling, a sloe-thorn sprang from the play and put out Midir's eye; he stayed a year in the mound while Dían Cécht, the physician of the Túatha Dé Danann, made him whole. For his reward and his heart's desire he named Étaín Echraide, daughter of Ailill, the fairest woman in Ireland — and it was Óengus who went to win her. Her father Ailill mac Máta, king of the Ulaid, set a bride-price no mortal could pay: twelve plains cleared of their stones and wood, and twelve rivers led out of the land to the sea. Óengus performed the labors with the Dagda's strength behind him, and Midir brought Étaín home to Brí Léith as his wife. The tale's arithmetic is exact: the god's first possession of Étaín was bought by service, the price of a wounded eye — and it was the one part of the story that ended peaceably. [Tochmarc Étaíne] The Fly in the Crystal Bower: Midir already had a wife: Fuamnach, foster-daughter of Bresal the druid, and versed in her foster-father's arts. When Étaín came home to Brí Léith, Fuamnach's jealousy found its instrument — a rod of scarlet quicken-tree — and one stroke made her rival a pool of water, then a worm, then a purple fly of wondrous size and sweetness. For seven years the fly that was Étaín went with Midir wherever he went, and he knew her in her shape; but Fuamnach's malice outlasted his keeping. The fly came at last to Brú na Bóinne, where Óengus knew her and built her a grianán, a crystal sun-bower filled with healing herbs — until Fuamnach raised a magic wind that swept her across Ireland for seven years more, to fall into the cup of the wife of Étar, an Ulster warrior, at the Bay of Cíú. She was drunk, conceived, and born again a thousand and twelve years after her first birth: Étaín, daughter of Étar. Midir's house is the still center of the storm — the husband whose hall became the battlefield of two women's powers, and who waited out the centuries the tale demanded of him. [Tochmarc Étaíne] The Long Game at Tara: In her second life Étaín married Eochaid Airem, high king of Ireland at Tara, and Midir came for her as the tale had promised. First he came in the shape of Ailill Anglonnach, the king's brother, who was wasting with love of her — three nights he lay beside her in that likeness and did not touch her, and so saved both her honor and Ailill's life. Then he revealed himself and asked her to come away with him; she answered that she would not go without her husband's leave. So Midir took the leave the hard way. He came to Tara and challenged Eochaid to fidchell. Game after game Midir lost, and paid the stakes without stint — horses and treasures in such plenty that the king's greed was schooled by the god's purse. Then the board was set once more, and the stake named was an embrace and a kiss from Étaín; Midir won. Eochaid deferred the payment for a month, and when the month was out Tara stood ringed with warriors and the house barred. Midir appeared all the same in the midst of the hall, sang to Étaín the invitation to the wondrous land, took her in his arms, and the two rose through the smoke-hole as two swans linked by a silver chain, while the host of Ireland watched from the ramparts and could do nothing. [Tochmarc Étaíne] The Fifty Women in One Likeness: Eochaid's answer was the spade: he set the men of Ireland to digging up the síd-mounds one by one, a war of delving against the hollow hills, until the host stood over Brí Léith itself. Then Midir came to the parley, and the bargain struck was surrender of a kind: on the morrow fifty women came out of the mound, every one of them in Étaín's exact likeness, and the king was told to choose his wife. He chose — and chose his own daughter, born to Étaín in the síd and hidden in the likeness of her mother. By that unwitting union a daughter was conceived who was exposed and spared, reared as Mess Búachalla, the cowherd's fosterling, and through her the line ran down to Conaire Mór, the doomed king of the Bruiden Da Derga. When Midir revealed the deception he gave back the true Étaín as well; the tale lets the god keep the last word and the king keep his shame. It is the Otherworld's coldest jest: the wager was never about the game, and the digging was never going to win. [De Gabáil in t-Sída] The Foster-Father of the Young God: Behind the wooing stands the fosterage. When the Dagda divided the síd-mounds of Ireland among the Túatha Dé Danann, his son Óengus was away with Midir of Brí Léith, being fostered, and received nothing — the absence that led to the famous quibble of the day and the night, and to Brú na Bóinne passing to the son. The tradition thus ties the two mounds together from the beginning: the young god reared at Brí Léith, the proud god's eye healed at the Brug. The foster-bond runs both ways through the dossier. It was for Midir that Óengus won Étaín Echraide and performed her father's labors; it was in Óengus's bower that Étaín the purple fly found her one refuge. Irish fosterage was no light tie — it stood beside blood, and the tales honor it. Midir's proudest title is not lord of Brí Léith but the one the stories keep proving: the man who raised the son of the young.
